Hi Zoe, Marissa —

Thanks for the clear questions. Below is a concise technical summary and the current operational posture. I attached our DR_runbook.pdf (redacted version) for reference.

1) Backup types and retention
- Hot incremental snapshots: continuous/incremental KV snapshots kept for 90 days by default. Designed for fast point-in-time recovery.
- Cold archival snapshots: weekly full backups kept up to 12 months (configurable per-customer depending on plan).
- Immutable storage: backups are stored on object storage with WORM-like write-once semantics for the configured retention window; we do not alter historical snapshot files once written.

2) Deletion semantics and "propagation"
- Active data store: when a customer issues a deletion, Redwood marks the object(s) as deleted (tombstone) and purges the active storage according to our deletion pipeline and any agreed retention hold. This change is immediate for active traffic.
- Backups: because snapshots are immutable, deleting in active storage does not retroactively remove content from already-created snapshots. In other words, a point-in-time restore to a timestamp before the deletion will include the deleted data.

3) Options to address this for compliance/legal needs
- Targeted backup sanitization: for contractual or legal obligations, Redwood can execute a targeted purge workflow that (a) identifies snapshots containing the deleted objects, (b) rehydrates those snapshots in a controlled environment, (c) scrubbers/transformations remove the deleted objects, and (d) new sanitized snapshots replace the originals. This is an operational process with an SLA (see timeline below) and is only performed with proper authorization and auditing.
- Configurable retention policies: for customers requiring no historical retention of specific data types, we offer shorter snapshot retention windows or an opt-in policy on Private deployments where backups are customer-controlled.

4) Timelines & proof
- Typical targeted sanitization run: 14–30 business days depending on snapshot size and retention footprint. We provide an audit package that includes logs of the sanitization job, hashes of removed objects, and verification steps.

5) DR restores and safety controls
- Restores are point-in-time. By default, a restore to a time prior to deletion will include the deleted data. We have an internal gate: before any restore that could reintroduce deleted data into active production, we run a pre-restore policy check and can either block the restore or perform an immediate post-restore sanitization.

6) Contract language & addenda
- Our standard SOC2/DR statement outlines retention defaults. For customers like Acme with PHI/regulated requirements, we can add a Data Deletion & Backup Purge addendum to the contract specifying purge SLAs, proof-of-deletion artifacts, and any additional costs.

Links / docs attached: DR_runbook.pdf (redacted), sample SOC2 excerpt.

If helpful, we'll draft a short playbook excerpt Acme can hold for legal.

Hi Zoe — quick follow-up to your two points:

1) Guarantee on restores: operationally, we cannot erase the fact that a restore to a pre-deletion point contains the data — restores are by definition point-in-time. However, we enforce the following safeguards to avoid accidental reintroduction:
   - Pre-restore policy check that flags restores which include deleted entities.
   - Block-by-default option: for accounts with the "strict deletion" flag, restores that would reintroduce deleted objects are blocked unless Acme explicitly approves (written approval via email or DocuSign).
   - Post-restore sanitization: when requested, we will run the targeted sanitization on the restored environment before it is promoted back to production.

2) Authorization & audit trail: the targeted sanitization workflow requires a formal request from an authorized Acme contact (InfoSec or Legal), confirmation from the Redwood account owner (Marissa or her manager), and approval from our Security operations lead. Every step is logged; the audit package includes who authorized, timestamps, job IDs, and checksums/hashes of removed objects.

Operational SLA we propose for the DPA addendum:
- Acknowledgement within 2 business days.
- Completion of identification and scope within 7 business days.
- Complete sanitization and delivery of audit package within 30 calendar days (dependent on snapshot size).

I'll attach a short excerpt (deletion_playbook_excerpt.txt) that you can drop into the DPA. If this looks good, Marissa can draft a MAP and we can get the engagement started.

— Rishi
